title: Seva with neighbors
hookLine: serving alongside people of every faith
tomorrow: creek, food bank, tutoring: Simran can't keep all three. which one?

lines: WHY IS FARID IN THE GRANTH?
cards: Simran stays. The van belongs to a church youth group in matching orange shirts, and Maya's cousin climbs out of it. By noon a family from the mosque across town shows up with a cooler of water.
So Simran is sorting cans beside a boy wearing a cross, and she remembers something odd in her own gutka.
Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib there are shaloks signed with a name that isn't a Guru's: Farid, a Muslim Sufi. In the Sikh scripture. Why is he there?

teach.b: Farid isn't alone. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the words of the Gurus and also of bhagats, saints from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, among them Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Farid.
Guru Arjan, who compiled it, set their hymns inside the Sikh scripture itself.
Here's one way to solve the puzzle, from Guru Arjan's own words on Ang 1299, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone.
And in Akal Ustat, a composition tradition credits to Guru Gobind Singh, there's a line Sikhs hold close: manas ki jaat sabhai ekai pahichanbo.
Recognize the whole human race as one. So the book on the gurdwara's throne is already a shared table. But it's not a blur.

teach.h: SIDE BY SIDE, NOT A BLUR.
teach.b: Farid's verses keep his name, and in places a Guru's shalok answers his, side by side, with the Gurus' teaching as the frame. That's seva with neighbors too.
Simran doesn't stop being a Sikh to carry a bag next to a Christian kid or a Muslim family. She brings her reasons, they bring theirs, and the creek gets clean.
One to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh scripture has a Muslim saint's verses inside it.

how: Sikh groups join interfaith service days, food drives and relief work alongside churches, mosques, temples and synagogues, and the gurdwara langar is open to anyone who comes.

o: serving beside people of other faiths, side by side
joining one big blended religion for good causes
turning every service day into a chance to preach

games.q: neighbors in the Granth — tap the pairs.
p: saints whose hymns sit in the Granth
a Muslim Sufi with shaloks inside
recognize the human race as one

s: the Guru Granth Sahib contains only the Sikh Gurus' own words
it also holds hymns of bhagats from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, Farid among them.
serving beside another faith's group means blending the two into one
Farid's verses keep his name, with the Gurus' teaching as the frame: side by side, not a blur.
Akal Ustat says to recognize the whole human race as one
manas ki jaat sabhai ekai pahichanbo, in a composition tradition credits to Guru Gobind Singh.

games.q: a temple and a church are running a joint coat drive, and your gurdwara is invited. someone says, 'we should do our own drive so nobody gets confused.' what fits today?
o: join in. no one is a stranger, and you can serve with your own reasons.
run a separate drive, so the Sikh part stays clear.
join, but leave anything Sikh at home so it stays neutral.
games.why: Guru Arjan wrote that no one is an enemy or a stranger, and put other saints' hymns inside the Granth, side by side and still distinct.

practice: Run a small plan in your head during the sit. First the wish: one project near you where neighbors of other faiths already serve, a food pantry, a park day, a blood drive. Then the one thing most likely to stop you joining.
Then the plan: when that obstacle shows up, what you'll do instead.

wordCard.voice: Seva with neighbors. Serving beside people of every faith, keeping your own reasons, because no one is a stranger.

orig.note: from Akal Ustat: the human race; the line asks you to recognize it as one.

carryVoice: Keep this one: serve together, with your reasons and theirs, and one creek between you. See you tomorrow.
